intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, tells you what to remember and warns you where people slip. Work the section exercises in pencil, check yourself against the recall questions, and write your own notes in the margins.

sections.title: What rights are and where they come from
sections.big_idea: A human right is **a claim with a duty attached**, held against a named duty-bearer who owes respect, protection and fulfilment.
in_plain_words: A wish becomes a right when someone is obliged to act and a route to a remedy exists. The rights-holder makes the claim; the duty-bearer, usually the state, owes it. The duty has three layers: respect (do not interfere), protect (stop third parties) and fulfil (take positive steps).

Rights come from philosophy, international law and domestic law, and for field work the domestic source is where they bite hardest. The Vienna Declaration calls them universal, indivisible, interdependent and interrelated. **Rights language adds a duty-bearer, a legal standard, a remedy and non-discrimination to needs language.**

key_terms.meaning: The person or group who can make the claim.
The body that owes the duty, first the state.
The three layers of state obligation.
All rights have equal status, with no hierarchy.
Right to go straight to the Supreme Court for a fundamental right.
A right framed for a group, such as self-determination.

worked_example.title: Map your work onto the three layers
worked_example.setup: Use the right to food and three programme activities.
steps: Monitoring ration shops stops traders diverting grain: the protect layer.
Helping families get ration cards means positive steps: the fulfil layer.
Documenting evictions that destroy crops or block access to common land speaks to the respect layer.
For each activity, name the rights-holder and the duty-bearer, such as the food department.
worked_example.answer: Protect, fulfil and respect, each with a named duty-bearer and a remedy to pursue.

mistakes: Calling a demand for a road a right, when no named authority owes it.
Treating civil rights as a luxury that follows growth, or food and housing as charity.
Assuming a group decision speaks for everyone in the group.
Relying on philosophy when only domestic or international law has a forum.

recall.q: What is a human right, in the deck's definition?
recall.a: A legal and moral entitlement held by every person, matched by a duty-bearer's obligation, with some route to a remedy.

recall.q: What are the three layers of state duty?
recall.a: Respect, protect and fulfil.

recall.q: What did the Vienna Declaration of 1993 say?
recall.a: All human rights are universal, indivisible and interdependent and interrelated.

recall.q: Which articles give access to the Supreme Court and High Courts?
recall.a: Article 32 for the Supreme Court and Article 226 for High Court writs.

recall.q: What four things does rights language add to needs language?
recall.a: A named duty-bearer, a legal standard, a remedy and non-discrimination.

sections.title: The international bill of rights
sections.big_idea: The UDHR set the standard in 1948, and the **two Covenants of 1966** turned it into treaties.
in_plain_words: The Universal Declaration was adopted on 10 December 1948 with no vote against and eight abstentions. It is a resolution, so its force comes from treaties built on it, constitutions that copied it and customary law. Hansa Mehta changed 'all men' to 'all human beings' in Article 1.

The ICCPR and ICESCR followed on 16 December 1966, eighteen years later. The ICCPR is immediate, with limits that must be lawful, aimed at a legitimate purpose, necessary and proportionate. **The ICESCR asks for progressive realisation but also a minimum core that applies at once.** Soft law such as general comments guides how both are read.

diagram.note: the three are often called the International Bill of Human Rights

key_terms.meaning: Universal Declaration of Human Rights, 1948.
International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.
International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.
Taking steps to the maximum of available resources.
The part of each right that applies immediately.
Suspending a right in a public emergency, never from life or torture.

worked_example.title: Years and the four-step test
worked_example.setup: Use the dates in the deck and test a restriction on a peaceful protest.
steps: Years from the UDHR to the Covenants: 1966 − 1948 = 18.
Is the restriction set out in law?
Does it serve a legitimate aim such as public order?
Is it necessary, with a pressing need, and proportionate, the least restrictive option that works?
worked_example.answer: Eighteen years; the restriction stands only if it passes all four steps.

mistakes: Reading Article 2(1) of the ICESCR as permission to wait.
Treating the UDHR as a binding treaty.
Applying the four-step test to rights that are absolute, such as freedom from torture.
Citing soft law as if it were hard law without the Indian court route.

recall.q: On what date was the UDHR adopted and by which resolution?
recall.a: 10 December 1948, GA resolution 217 A (III).

recall.q: When did the ICESCR and ICCPR enter into force?
recall.a: 3 January 1976 and 23 March 1976.

recall.q: What does the minimum core include?
recall.a: Basic food, essential primary health care, basic shelter and the most basic forms of education.

recall.q: Which rights can never be limited?
recall.a: Freedom from torture and slavery, among the absolute rights.

recall.q: What did the Supreme Court do with CEDAW in Vishaka?
recall.a: Read it into fundamental rights where no Indian law conflicted.

sections.title: Core treaties and ratification
sections.big_idea: India is party to **six of the nine** core UN treaties, and has accepted no individual complaints procedure.
in_plain_words: Nine core treaties each have a committee of independent experts. A state signs to show intent and becomes a party by ratification or accession. India acceded to both Covenants on 10 April 1979, and has signed the torture and enforced disappearance conventions without ratifying either.

The neighbours differ: Bangladesh and Sri Lanka are party to all nine, Nepal and Pakistan to seven. States join on stated terms through reservations and declarations, and those mark where national law and the treaty diverge. **The CEDAW reservations sit where the treaty meets religious personal law.**

diagram.root: India and the nine core treaties
diagram.caption: status as of October 2026

key_terms.meaning: Joining a treaty without having signed first.
Becoming a party after signing.
Excludes or changes the legal effect of a provision.
States how the state reads a provision.
Convention on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women.
Source of ratification status by country.

worked_example.title: Count the gaps
worked_example.setup: Use the number of core treaties joined by each state, out of nine.
steps: India has joined six: 9 − 6 = 3 missing (CAT, CED and CMW).
Nepal has joined seven: 9 − 7 = 2 missing (CMW and CED).
Pakistan has also joined seven: 9 − 7 = 2 missing.
Bangladesh and Sri Lanka have joined all nine: 9 − 9 = 0 missing.
worked_example.answer: India misses three, Nepal and Pakistan two each, and Bangladesh and Sri Lanka none.

mistakes: Treating a signature as a binding commitment.
Taking a count of ratifications as a measure of practice.
Forgetting that all four neighbours have joined the torture convention which India has not.
Assuming a person in India can bring an individual complaint to a UN committee.

recall.q: How many core treaties is India party to?
recall.a: Six: CERD, ICCPR, ICESCR, CEDAW, CRC and CRPD.

recall.q: When did India accede to both Covenants?
recall.a: 10 April 1979.

recall.q: What did India declare on Article 1 of both Covenants?
recall.a: Self-determination applies only to peoples under foreign domination.

recall.q: What is the difference between a reservation and an interpretative declaration?
recall.a: A reservation excludes or changes a provision's legal effect. A declaration states how the state reads it.

recall.q: Why do CEDAW reservations matter to programmes?
recall.a: They mark where the treaty meets personal law on marriage, divorce and inheritance.

sections.title: The UN machinery
sections.big_idea: The UN **persuades and rarely compels**, and works best when it backs a domestic campaign with evidence and allies.
in_plain_words: The Human Rights Council, created in 2006, has 47 state members, so its decisions are political. The Universal Periodic Review examines every state in turn: inputs, dialogue, recommendations, response and follow-up. India's 2022 review produced 339 recommendations, and the torture convention ones were noted.

Treaty bodies review reports and issue concluding observations, special procedures send communications and write thematic reports, and individual complaints work only where accepted, which excludes India. **Use supported UPR recommendations as public commitments you can quote back to officials.**

diagram.caption: five mechanisms and what each produces

key_terms.meaning: Universal Periodic Review of every state by other states.
A treaty body's findings after reviewing a state.
A treaty body's reading of a treaty article.
An alternative report from civil society.
Independent expert on a theme or country.
A state's response when it declines a recommendation.

worked_example.title: Council seats, then pick the mechanism
worked_example.setup: Use the Council's 47 seats and four programme needs.
steps: Add the regional seats: 13 + 13 + 6 = 32.
Then 32 + 8 + 7 = 47 seats in total.
Hold the government to a public commitment: the UPR.
Need a sector benchmark or shadow report: a treaty body. An urgent case: a special procedure.
An individual complaint to a UN committee is not available for India.
worked_example.answer: 47 seats; UPR for commitments, treaty bodies for benchmarks, special procedures for urgent cases.

mistakes: Expecting the Council to take direct action on a local case.
Assuming a state must accept every UPR recommendation.
Travelling to Geneva before using domestic routes.
Planning an individual complaint to a UN body for a case in India.

recall.q: When was the Human Rights Council created and by which resolution?
recall.a: 2006, by GA resolution 60/251.

recall.q: How many recommendations did India receive in 2022?
How long are Council terms?
recall.a: Three years, with no immediate re-election after two consecutive terms.

recall.q: What do treaty bodies do?
recall.a: Review state reports, write general comments, hear individual complaints where accepted, and some run inquiries.

recall.q: How many thematic and country mandates did special procedures have in August 2026?
recall.a: 44 thematic and 12 country mandates.

sections.title: The human rights-based approach
sections.big_idea: A rights-based approach changes **who decides, who pays over time and who is answerable**, not only what is delivered.
in_plain_words: In 2003 UN agencies agreed three points: programmes further the realisation of rights, standards and principles guide all phases, and capacity is built for duty-bearers to meet obligations and rights-holders to claim. Six principles turn this into questions about coverage, trade-offs, interdependence, disaggregation, participation and accountability.

A common method uses three analyses: causes, roles and capacity gaps. The approach has fair critics: relabelling, legalism, the state as violator and resource limits. **Test any design by asking whether activities, indicators and reporting lines changed.**

diagram.caption: three linked analyses at the start of a design

key_terms.meaning: The 2003 UN statement of what a rights-based approach means.
A legal space such as a gram sabha or school committee.
A tool such as RTI, public hearing or grievance portal.
Adding the word rights without changing design.
Pushing conflicts into slow, costly courts.

worked_example.title: Review a hand-pump programme
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a trust installs pumps in 40 hamlets, and two Dalit hamlets had pumps sited at the dominant-caste end.
steps: Share of hamlets affected: 2 ÷ 40 = 5%.
Cause: the trust picked sites. Fix: hamlet meetings with women and Dalit households choose sites.
Cause: repairs depend on the trust. Fix: use the panchayat repair budget and train a local mechanic.
Cause: reports count pumps only. Fix: also report access by caste and gender.
worked_example.answer: A 5% share hides a breach of non-discrimination; the fixes change who decides, who pays and who answers.

mistakes: Claiming participation and accountability without showing them.
Treating exclusion as a coverage gap to close later.
Building a violator state's capacity without a risk analysis.
Promising more than the budget can deliver.

recall.q: What are the three points of the 2003 Common Understanding?
recall.a: Further realisation of rights; standards guide all phases; build capacity of duty-bearers and rights-holders.

recall.q: Name two principles and the question each raises.
recall.a: Universality: who is outside our coverage? Accountability: is there a grievance route that works?

recall.q: What are the four criticisms in the deck?
recall.a: Relabelling, legalism, the state as violator and resource limits.

recall.q: What is the test for any programme on rights-holders?
recall.a: Could they find out what they are entitled to, complain, and get an answer?

recall.q: What changes in the water programme after the review?
recall.a: Who decides, who pays over time and who is answerable.

sections.title: Rights in the Indian Constitution
sections.big_idea: Article 21, read with Part IV, **carries most social rights** in Indian law.
in_plain_words: Part III lists enforceable fundamental rights, and Article 32 is itself a fundamental right. Part IV lists directive principles that no court enforces, but courts read them into Part III. Gopalan (1950) treated rights as separate compartments, and Maneka Gandhi (1978) required that procedure be fair.

Article 21 then grew: speedy trial, dignity, livelihood, education, custodial compensation, emergency treatment and privacy. Olga Tellis, Puttaswamy, the RTE Act and Vishaka show the main routes. **Treaties enter Indian courts only where Indian law is silent.**

key_terms.meaning: Enforceable rights in Part III.
Goals in Part IV that the state must pursue.
Gopalan's reading of Article 21.
A test of law, legitimate aim and means in proportion.
Free and compulsory education for ages 6 to 14.
A treaty needs legislation before it changes domestic law.

worked_example.title: From the quota to the classroom
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a private unaided school has 80 seats in Class I. The RTE Act requires at least 25 per cent for weaker sections and disadvantaged groups.
steps: Seats reserved: 80 × 25 ÷ 100 = 20.
The gap between Gopalan and Maneka: 1978 − 1950 = 28 years.
The families need to know about the quota, complete the application and appeal a refusal.
States must reimburse schools for the quota to work.
worked_example.answer: At least 20 seats; helping families apply and appeal is direct rights work.

mistakes: Treating Part IV as irrelevant because no court enforces it.
Relying on a treaty when a clear Indian statute says otherwise.
Quoting Olga Tellis as banning all evictions.
Forgetting that data-heavy work now raises constitutional privacy questions.

recall.q: What did Maneka Gandhi (1978) establish?
recall.a: Articles 14, 19 and 21 must be read together, and procedure must be reasonable.

recall.q: What did Olga Tellis hold?
recall.a: The right to life includes livelihood, and fair procedure applies before eviction.

recall.q: What test did Puttaswamy (2017) set for intrusions into privacy?
recall.a: A law, a legitimate state aim and proportionality.

recall.q: What does the RTE Act require of private unaided schools?
recall.a: At least 25 per cent of Class I seats for weaker sections and disadvantaged groups.

recall.q: What does Vishaka show about treaties?
recall.a: The Court drew on CEDAW to frame guidelines until Parliament legislated.

sections.title: Courts, PIL and commissions
sections.big_idea: PIL opened the courts, and the **one-year bar** is the rule most often missed with commissions.
in_plain_words: Public interest litigation relaxed standing so anyone acting in good faith could bring a case for people too marginalised to do so. Courts treated letters as petitions and used continuing mandamus, commissioners, guidelines, compensation and fact-finding. Litigation helps when an entitlement is clear and hurts when communities did not choose it.

The Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 created the NHRC and SHRCs. The NHRC can inquire, visit jails and recommend, but its recommendations are not binding. **It cannot inquire into matters more than one year old.** Neighbouring countries have their own constitutional routes with limitation periods.

left.title: NHRC powers
items: Inquire suo motu or on petition
Visit jails and places of detention

right.title: NHRC limits
items: No inquiry into matters over one year old
Armed forces: report and recommend only
Cannot take matters pending before another commission

key_terms.meaning: Public interest litigation brought on behalf of others.
The court keeps the case open and issues orders over years.
National Human Rights Commission.
State Human Rights Commission.
Standards for national human rights institutions.
Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions.

worked_example.title: Count the days to file
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: custodial harm occurs on 3 March 2026.
steps: Document the dates, names, medical and police papers at once.
The one-year limit runs: 2026 + 1 = 2027, so file before 3 March 2027.
File with the SHRC first, since the NHRC can transfer to the state commission.
If relief is refused, a High Court writ remains.
worked_example.answer: File with the SHRC before 3 March 2027, with a dated record kept from the start.

mistakes: Waiting past one year to file with the commission.
Going to court when officials could fix a problem with a letter or RTI.
Treating NHRC recommendations as binding orders.
Citing India's GANHRI status without checking the latest decision.

recall.q: Which case set the PIL standing principle?
recall.a: S.P. Gupta v President of India (1981).

recall.q: What did Hussainara Khatoon concern?
recall.a: Undertrials held for years in Bihar jails; the Court ordered release on personal bond.

recall.q: What is section 36(2)?
recall.a: The one-year bar on inquiry into old matters.

recall.q: What is India's NHRC status?
recall.a: Accredited A, with a downgrade to B recommended in March 2025 and review postponed to November 2026.

recall.q: Which court route does Sri Lanka's Article 126 offer?
recall.a: Supreme Court petition for executive infringement, within one month.

sections.title: Economic and social rights in practice
sections.big_idea: A rights reading of food, health, work and housing asks about the **minimum core, the trend and the poorest**.
in_plain_words: The right to food grew from PUCL into the National Food Security Act 2013, which gives an entitlement that can be claimed. Paschim Banga (1996) held that lack of resources cannot excuse failing to provide emergency treatment. Olga Tellis tied shelter to Article 21 and required fair procedure before removal.

Work and social security changed in 2025 and 2026 with the repeal of MGNREGA and the Labour Codes. OHCHR's structural, process and outcome indicators give a monitoring shape, and budgets are evidence. **Disaggregation turns an ordinary indicator into a rights indicator.**

children.label: Outcome
items: Class 8 completion by girls and Dalit children

key_terms.meaning: The immediate floor of each right.
The rapporteur's guidance on development-based evictions.
Whether laws and institutions exist.
Effort: budgets, programmes, coverage.
Result for rights-holders.
A cut that needs justification.

worked_example.title: Read a budget as a rights document
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a scheme pays ₹6,000 to each of 50,000 eligible women, and the allocation is ₹24 crore.
steps: Cost of the entitlement: 50,000 × 6,000 = 300,000,000 rupees.
Shortfall: 30 − 24 = 6 crore.
Share of the entitlement funded: 24 ÷ 30 = 80%.
worked_example.answer: The scheme funds 80% of its promise, a ₹6 crore gap to explain under progressive realisation.

mistakes: Reading a high stunting rate without asking whether the trend is down and the poorest are improving.
Comparing stunting across countries as if the surveys were from the same year.
Advising on rural employment without reading the new Act.
Treating an average that rises as proof of non-discrimination.

recall.q: Which case turned food schemes into entitlements?
recall.a: PUCL v Union of India, WP (C) 196 of 2001.

recall.q: What did Paschim Banga hold?
recall.a: Lack of resources cannot excuse failing to provide emergency treatment; Article 21 was breached.

recall.q: What replaced the MGNREGA from 1 July 2026?
recall.a: The Viksit Bharat G RAM G Act 2025, with 125 days of work.

recall.q: What are the four budget questions?
recall.a: Allocation, release and spending, equity, and backward steps.

recall.q: What was India's stunting figure in NFHS-6?
recall.a: 29.3 per cent, down from 35.5 per cent in NFHS-5.

sections.title: Civic space and its legal framework
sections.big_idea: The law on speech, assembly, association and funding decides **how an NGO is funded and what risks communities take**.
in_plain_words: Expression, assembly and association are protected by ICCPR Articles 19, 21 and 22 and by Article 19(1)(a), (b) and (c) of the Constitution, each with permitted grounds for restriction. Sedition under 124A has been replaced by section 152 of the BNS, which courts are still reading.

The UAPA restricts bail and allows long investigations. The FCRA 2010 as amended in 2020 bars onward transfer, caps administrative costs at 20 per cent and fixes the receiving account. The DPDP Act changed RTI section 8(1)(j) from 13 November 2025. **Compliance and a risk plan protect the people you work with.**

key_terms.meaning: Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act 2010.
Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act 1967.
Act endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity.
The UAPA bail restriction.
RTI exemption for personal information.
A person promoting the protection of human rights.

worked_example.title: Apply the FCRA cap
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: an organisation receives ₹50 lakh of foreign contribution in a year.
steps: Administrative cap at 20%: 50 × 20 ÷ 100 = 10 lakh.
Left for programme costs: 50 − 10 = 40 lakh.
Onward transfer to a partner NGO is barred, so no part can be sub-granted.
Receipt must be in an FCRA account at the specified SBI branch in New Delhi.
worked_example.answer: At most ₹10 lakh for administration, ₹40 lakh for programme, and no sub-granting.

mistakes: Assuming sedition survives under its old name in the BNS.
Sub-granting foreign funds to a partner NGO.
Naming officials or beneficiaries in RTI requests now that the exemption has widened.
Asking people to speak up before planning for retaliation.

recall.q: Which Indian article protects assembly?
recall.a: Article 19(1)(b), with restrictions under 19(3).

recall.q: What did the Supreme Court order in Vombatkere on 11 May 2022?
recall.a: Governments were expected to refrain from FIRs under 124A while it was reconsidered.

recall.q: What does Najeeb say about the UAPA bail bar?
recall.a: It does not oust constitutional courts' power to grant bail for Part III violations.

recall.q: What is the FCRA administrative expense cap?
recall.a: 20 per cent of foreign contribution in a year.

recall.q: What date did the RTI amendment take effect?
recall.a: 13 November 2025.

sections.title: Business and human rights
sections.big_idea: The UNGPs rest on **three pillars**, and human rights due diligence is the company's duty to find and address harm.
in_plain_words: The Human Rights Council endorsed the Guiding Principles on 16 June 2011. Pillar I is the state duty to protect, Pillar II the corporate responsibility to respect, and Pillar III access to remedy. They are not a treaty; their force comes from national law, company policy, investor rules and supply-chain contracts.

Due diligence has four steps: assess, integrate, track and communicate. A grievance mechanism works if it meets eight tests. India's framework includes the 2019 zero draft action plan, the 2018 guidelines, the BRSR and CSR duty. **After Rana Plaza, worker voice became the mechanism programmes can strengthen.**

key_terms.meaning: UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, 2011.
Identify, prevent, mitigate and account for adverse impacts.
Criteria for effective grievance mechanisms.
SEBI's sustainability report, mandatory for the top 1,000.
Garment factory collapse near Dhaka in April 2013.
Ability to refuse unsafe work and report without retaliation.

worked_example.title: Test a company hotline
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a company hotline is run by the company, published in English only, and has no stated timelines.
steps: Legitimate: would workers use it without fear? Doubtful.
Accessible: is it in local languages? No.
Predictable: are deadlines published? No.
Count the failures: that is 3 of the first 3 tests, so 8 − 3 = 5 tests remain to check.
Decide what to ask the company to change before partnering.
worked_example.answer: The hotline fails three tests, and the NGO should ask for changes or an independent route first.

mistakes: Treating the UNGPs as a treaty.
Running a company's grievance system with no independence.
Using CSR funds to deliver services the state must provide, with no exit plan.
Signing confidentiality terms that prevent reporting harm.

recall.q: Name the three pillars.
recall.a: The state duty to protect, the corporate responsibility to respect, and access to remedy.

recall.q: Which principle sets the grievance mechanism criteria?
recall.a: Principle 31.

recall.q: When did Rana Plaza collapse?
recall.a: 24 April 2013.

recall.q: What is the status of India's National Action Plan?
recall.a: A 2019 zero draft that is not adopted as of October 2026.

recall.q: What should an NGO review before a CSR partnership?
recall.a: The company's due diligence and disclosures.

sections.title: Using rights in a programme
sections.big_idea: A rights-based workplan gives every problem **a law, a named office and an action**.
in_plain_words: Run the design checklist at design stage and at mid-term: which rights, which duty-bearers, who is excluded, how people take part, what grievance route works, what the state already owes, what could go wrong, and who sustains the gains.

The Bihar example shows the shape, and the decision table matches problems to routes. Documentation must be consented, minimal and secure. A good letter has five parts. **Rights indicators measure duty-bearer performance and equality of access**, and the do-no-harm plan keeps the decision with the person at risk.

diagram.caption: a rights-based letter in five parts

key_terms.meaning: Matches a problem to a first route and a fallback.
Splitting indicators by sex, caste or tribe, and disability.
A record of who holds the originals.
Punishment of complainants by officials or elites.
Results framework built on duty-bearer performance.

worked_example.title: Size a restoration request
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 14 households with 4 people each lost ration cards on 3 March.
steps: People affected: 14 × 4 = 56.
Monthly grain under section 3(1) at 5 kg each: 56 × 5 = 280 kg.
Letter: state the facts, cite section 3(1), name the office, request restoration within 15 days.
If no reply: an RTI request on the file and a copy to the district collector.
worked_example.answer: 56 people and 280 kg a month at stake, written as a dated request.

mistakes: Going to court first when a written application would work.
Posting identifiable images of survivors or names on messaging groups.
Measuring trainings held rather than grievances resolved on time.
Promising outcomes the programme cannot deliver.

recall.q: Which route is first for a denied scheme benefit?
recall.a: A written application or grievance portal.

recall.q: What is the first route for information withheld?
recall.a: An RTI request, answered in 30 days.

recall.q: What is the rights-based version of 'children enrolled'?
recall.a: Children completing Class 8, by sex, caste and disability.

recall.q: Name two risks in the do-no-harm list.
recall.a: Retaliation against complainants, and exposure of identities through data leaks.

recall.q: Who decides whether to complain?
recall.a: The person whose rights were violated.

sections.title: Summing up and where next
sections.big_idea: Start with **domestic routes**, check time-sensitive facts, and carry eight points into practice.
in_plain_words: On the law: a right is a claim with a named duty-bearer and a remedy; India is party to six of the nine core treaties; Article 21 with Part IV carries most social rights; treaties enter Indian courts where Indian law is silent.

On practice: start with letters, RTI, commissions and courts; file with an SHRC or the NHRC within one year; measure duty-bearer performance and equality; plan for retaliation and data protection. **Check GANHRI status, the DPDP and RTI litigation, the rural employment law and the Labour Codes**, which were all changing as of October 2026.

left.title: On the law
items: A right is a claim with a duty-bearer

key_terms.meaning: The office that owes the duty.
Letter, RTI, commission or court at home.
A status that may change after the deck was written.
A 101 course that extends one area.

worked_example.title: Choose the route
worked_example.setup: Match four situations to the decision table.
steps: Scheme benefit denied: a written application or grievance portal, then RTI on the file.
Information withheld: an RTI request in 30 days, then first appeal and the Information Commission.
Police abuse: medical record and complaint to a senior officer, then SHRC or NHRC within one year.
Systemic denial: collective representation, then a PIL with the affected people's consent.
worked_example.answer: Four situations, four first routes, and one deadline to remember: one year for commissions.

mistakes: Relying on Geneva alone when the pattern is local.
Quoting a status without checking the date.
Reading the deck as legal advice.
Skipping Child Rights before work with children.

recall.q: How many core treaties has India not joined?
recall.a: Three: CAT, CED and CMW.

recall.q: What is the suggested course order?
recall.a: Indian Constitution, then Governance & Accountability, then Advocacy Basics.

recall.q: Which course covers privacy after Puttaswamy?
recall.a: Digital Rights & AI 101.

recall.q: Which deadline applies to SHRC and NHRC complaints?
recall.a: One year.

recall.q: What should you read before any programme with children?
recall.a: Child Rights 101.

notes.2: The twelve sections run from the idea of a right, through international law and the UN, to the Indian Constitution, courts and commissions. Later sections apply them to economic and social rights, civic space and business, then to programme design. Skim the agenda and mark the sections closest to your own work.
notes.4: Hold the definition as a claim with a duty attached. A wish becomes a right when a named duty-bearer owes something and a remedy exists. Practise on a real case by naming the **rights-holder** and the **duty-bearer** for a problem in your area. If you cannot name the second, the claim is still a demand.
notes.5: Use respect, protect, fulfil as three questions about any right. The right to food example shows them: do not destroy crops, regulate traders who divert grain, run the public distribution system. Then **map your own work** onto the layers: monitoring ration shops is protect, and helping families get cards is fulfil.
notes.6: Know which of three sources you rely on, because each has its own forum. Philosophy gives force in argument, international law works through UN reviews, and domestic law is where rights bite hardest. Remember Articles 32 and 226, since **most remedies a programme uses sit in domestic law**.
notes.7: Memorise the 1993 wording: universal, indivisible, interdependent and interrelated. The practical reading is in the last paragraph: a family cannot vote freely if it fears losing its ration card, and a hungry child cannot use the right to education. So **civil and social rights have to be treated together**.
notes.8: Sort rights into two families and notice how India mirrors them: civil rights mostly in the enforceable Part III, economic and social goals mostly in the non-enforceable Part IV. The UDHR held both in one text, and the 1966 Covenants separated them. **Article 21 later drew them together**, as Section 06 shows.
notes.9: Check whether a right belongs to a person or a group. Self-determination, minority rights and forest community rights are collective. Consent changes at group level, since an individual can withdraw and a group needs a legitimate process. The caution: **group claims can hide unequal power inside the group**, so check both levels.
notes.10: Rights language adds four things to needs language: a named duty-bearer, a legal standard, a remedy and non-discrimination. Use the table to ask what each changes in your programme. The deck uses India as its main case and brings in **Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka** where their records differ.
notes.12: Remember 10 December 1948: no state voted against and eight abstained. The UDHR is a resolution and was never written as a binding treaty. Its force comes from the treaties built on it, from constitutions that copied its language, and from the argument that parts of it are **customary international law**.
notes.13: Use Hansa Mehta's change in Article 1 from 'all men' to 'all human beings' as a teaching story. It shows South Asian delegates shaped the text, which answers the claim that rights are a Western import. Opening a community session with it shows that **equality between women and men was argued for from this region**.
notes.14: Eighteen years separate the Declaration from the two Covenants of 1966. Learn the two in-force dates: the ICESCR on 3 January 1976 and the ICCPR on 23 March 1976. India's Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 names the 1966 date in its definition of the Covenants, which links the **statute to the treaties**.
notes.15: The ICCPR protects life, liberty, fair trial, privacy, expression, assembly, association and equality. Remember Article 2: rights apply immediately, without discrimination, with a remedy. Article 4 allows derogation in an emergency but never from life or torture. For civic space the test is: **provided by law, for a legitimate aim, and necessary**.
notes.16: ICESCR Article 2(1) asks states to realise rights progressively, to the maximum of available resources. Do not read it as permission to wait. It obliges a state to move forward, avoid going backwards without justification, and meet minimum core levels and non-discrimination at once. Ask whether **budgets and coverage are moving in the right direction**.
notes.17: Learn the minimum core: basic food, essential primary health care, basic shelter and the most basic education apply immediately. A state that falls short must show it used all resources as a priority. In the table, three obligations are immediate and one is progressive. Budget analysis is **one of the strongest rights tools** a programme has.
notes.18: Very few rights are absolute. Torture and slavery cannot be limited, and most others can be limited if the restriction passes four steps: lawful, legitimate aim, necessary, proportionate. Indian courts apply similar ideas through Article 19 and, since Puttaswamy (2017), proportionality. Use the four steps as a **checklist for any restriction** you meet.
notes.19: Soft law does not bind but guides. Keep the table at hand: Vienna 1993, the Paris Principles for bodies like the NHRC, the Common Understanding of 2003, the Guiding Principles of 2011 and general comments. Indian courts read such instruments into fundamental rights where no Indian law conflicts, so **soft law can become hard law**.
notes.21: Learn the nine treaties by acronym and year, and note that each has a committee of independent experts. A tenth body, the Subcommittee on Prevention of Torture, works under the optional protocol. Knowing the acronyms helps you read **UN reports on any South Asian country**.
notes.22: Signature shows intent, while ratification or accession binds. India acceded to both Covenants on 10 April 1979 and never signed them first. It signed the torture and enforced disappearance conventions and has ratified neither. The 2022 review's first recommendation asked it to **ratify what it has signed**, particularly the torture convention.
notes.23: Read the table down the status column: ratified, acceded, signed and not ratified, not signed. India is party to six of the nine. The note at the foot matters: **India has accepted no individual complaints procedure**, so a person in India cannot take an individual complaint to a UN treaty body.
notes.24: Compare India with its neighbours row by row. The (a) marks accession. All four neighbours have joined the torture convention, which India has not. Bangladesh acceded to the Convention on Enforced Disappearance in August 2024. Use the table to find **which standards an advocate can cite** in each country.
notes.25: Count the treaties: Bangladesh and Sri Lanka are party to all nine, Nepal and Pakistan to seven, India to six. A count is crude, because ratification says nothing about practice. It still shows **which UN committees can review a country** and which standards can be cited as binding. For India the missing torture convention matters most.
notes.26: A reservation excludes or changes the legal effect of a provision, and an interpretative declaration says how the state reads it. The label does not settle which it is. A reservation marks where national law and the treaty diverge, often **exactly where your programme will meet trouble**. Tracking withdrawal requests is low-cost advocacy.
notes.27: Read the table as a map of where Indian law and the Covenants diverge. The Article 1 declaration limits self-determination to peoples under foreign domination. The Article 9 declaration has been overtaken in part: since Nilabati Behera (1993) Indian courts **have awarded compensation for custodial violations** under Article 32.
notes.28: These CEDAW reservations sit where the treaty meets religious personal law, which governs marriage, divorce and inheritance. India declared on Articles 5(a), 16(1) and 16(2). Article 2 is the core obligation to eliminate discrimination and Article 16 covers marriage. Programmes on **child marriage, maintenance or inheritance** work in this gap.
notes.30: Memorise the structure: 47 states, elected individually by secret ballot, three-year terms, seats by region (13 Asian, 13 African, 6 Eastern European, 8 Latin American and Caribbean, 7 Western European and others). Its members are states, so **decisions are political as well as legal**. The Assembly can suspend a member for gross and systematic violations.
notes.31: Follow the five steps of the UPR: inputs, dialogue, recommendations, response, follow-up. Its strength is universality: every state is reviewed, so India is questioned on torture even without CAT. Its limit is that states review states, and a state can **note a recommendation without explanation**.
notes.32: India's 2022 review produced 339 recommendations from 130 delegations. Note that the recommendations to ratify the torture convention (151.1 and 151.2) were noted. The deck calls these a ready list of issues on which the government has not yet committed. Cite them by **recommendation number**.
notes.33: Read the UPR as a five-step toolkit for an NGO. Contribute to a coalition submission, brief embassies, extract supported recommendations, track progress and cite them by number. The effort column shows most steps are low effort. Recommendations a government supports are **public commitments you can quote back** in district meetings.
notes.34: Treaty bodies review state reports and issue concluding observations, write general comments, hear individual complaints where accepted, and run some inquiries. NGOs submit shadow reports, use concluding observations as benchmarks and quote general comments. Because reviews come years apart, **concluding observations stay useful** between reviews.
notes.35: Scan the table for the row and column that matter to you. India has accepted none of the individual complaints procedures, while Nepal and Sri Lanka have accepted several. A complaint can follow only after domestic remedies are exhausted. For India the consequence is clear: **violations are remedied at home** through courts, commissions and grievance routes.
notes.36: Special procedures are independent experts, with 44 thematic and 12 country mandates. They visit when invited, send communications on individual cases and report annually, and anyone can send information through OHCHR's online tool. Their thematic reports are a **free authoritative source of standards**, such as the rapporteur on adequate housing.
notes.37: Use this table to choose a mechanism by purpose. The Council is rarely direct, the UPR holds government to commitments, treaty bodies give sector benchmarks, special procedures suit urgent cases, and individual complaints apply only where accepted, which excludes India. Remember: **the UN system persuades and rarely compels**.
notes.39: The 2003 Common Understanding gives three checkable points: the goal is realising human rights, standards guide all programming in all phases, and capacity is built for duty-bearers to meet obligations and rights-holders to claim them. Use it as a **three-question audit** of any programme design.
notes.40: Treat the six principles as six questions: who is outside our coverage, are we trading one right against another, which other rights block our outcome, are results disaggregated, do communities shape design, is there a grievance route that works. The table gives each one. Pick the **two you cannot yet answer**.
notes.41: Compare the two framings row by row. Both deliver services. The rights-based version adds that people can claim, duty-bearers must perform better, the most excluded come first and accountability runs to communities and the state. The sharpest test: **will the public system keep delivering after project funding ends?**
notes.42: Learn the three-step method: causes, roles, capacity gaps. In the girls' schooling example, the causes include distance and safety, the roles include the school committee and the block office, and the gaps include parents' awareness and a transport budget. Design activities for **both sides of the relationship**: communities and officials.
notes.43: Participation and accountability are claimed most and shown least. Indian law gives hooks: gram sabhas, school management committees under RTE section 21, ward committees, and RTI requests answered within 30 days, or 48 hours for life or liberty. Use the test: could a rights-holder **find out, complain and get an answer**?
notes.44: This case is hypothetical. The trust installs pumps in 40 hamlets, and the review finds siting at the dominant-caste end in two Dalit hamlets, repairs dependent on the trust and an unused panchayat budget. The service is the same. What changed is **who decides, who pays over time and who is answerable**.
notes.45: Meet the four fair criticisms of the approach: relabelling, legalism, the state as violator and resource limits. Each shows a way it fails. Test for relabelling by asking whether activities, indicators and reporting lines changed. Where the state is the main threat, **run a risk analysis before building its capacity**.
notes.47: Scan Part III by article: 14 equality, 15 and 16 non-discrimination, 17 untouchability, 19 freedoms, 21 life and liberty, 21A education from 6 to 14, 23 and 24 forced labour and child labour, 25 to 30 religion and minorities, 32 remedy. Article 32 is **itself a fundamental right**, so the Supreme Court can be approached directly.
notes.48: Part IV sets goals the state must pursue, and Article 37 says they are enforceable by no court yet fundamental in governance. Keep a short list: 39A legal aid, 41 work and assistance, 42 conditions of work, 46 weaker sections, 47 nutrition. Welfare laws apply them, and **courts read them into Part III**.
notes.49: Two quotations mark the shift. Minerva Mills (1980) says the Constitution rests on a balance between Parts III and IV. Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1983, reported 1984) says the right to live with dignity draws on the Directive Principles. So an unenforceable directive like Article 47 **becomes enforceable through Article 21**.
notes.50: Compare Gopalan (1950), which treated each right as a separate compartment and accepted any procedure a valid law set out, with Maneka Gandhi (1978), which read Articles 14, 19 and 21 together. After 1978 the procedure must be right, just and fair. Maneka **opened the door to every later expansion of Article 21**.
notes.51: Use the table as a timeline of Article 21: speedy trial in 1979, dignity and nutrition in 1981, livelihood in 1985, education to age 14 in 1993, custodial compensation in 1993, emergency treatment in 1996, privacy in 2017. Together they turned a guarantee against unlawful detention into **the main source of social rights**.
notes.52: Olga Tellis (1985) held that the right to life includes the right to livelihood. The Court held that removal 'without notice' must be exercised reasonably, so fair procedure applies, and it left some evictions lawful. It is still cited on **notice and hearing**, and it shows the limits of litigation: a right recognised and removal still allowed.
notes.53: Puttaswamy (2017) is the privacy anchor: a nine-judge bench, with a three-part test of law, legitimate aim and proportionality. For data-heavy programmes consent, purpose limits and minimisation are **constitutional questions**. The DPDP Act 2023 follows, with duties applying from 13 May 2027. Check dates, since phases differ.
notes.54: Follow the four dates in order: Unni Krishnan (1993), the 86th Amendment inserting Article 21A (2002), the RTE Act (2009) and commencement on 1 April 2010. The RTE Act requires at least 25 per cent of Class I seats in private unaided schools for weaker sections. The quota works only if **families can apply and appeal**.
notes.55: India follows dualist practice: a treaty does not change domestic law until Parliament legislates (Article 253). Courts built a second route through Article 51(c) and the interpretation of fundamental rights, as in Vishaka (1997) with CEDAW. The limit: **a clear statute prevails over a treaty** in an Indian court.
notes.57: PIL relaxed the rule that only the injured person may sue. In S.P. Gupta (1981) Justice Bhagwati allowed any member of the public acting in good faith and with sufficient interest. Letters were treated as petitions, as in Nilabati Behera, and Hussainara Khatoon freed long-held undertrials. **Access to the court** changed first.
notes.58: Learn the five tools: continuing mandamus, court commissioners, guidelines pending a law, compensation and fact-finding. Each has an example in the table. The right to food case (PUCL, WP 196 of 2001) used continuing mandamus and commissioners. Use the table to see **what a court can order beyond one judgment**.
notes.59: Weigh litigation before filing. It tends to help with a clear denied entitlement, documented evidence and consent, many people affected, administrative routes exhausted, and a lawyer who can follow for years. It tends to hurt when communities did not choose it or officials could fix it with a letter. Treat a case as **one tool in a wider strategy**.
notes.60: The Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 created the NHRC and the SHRC framework. Its section 2(1)(d) definition ties human rights to the Constitution and the Covenants, enforceable by Courts in India. Learn the structure: a former Chief Justice or Supreme Court judge as chair, defined members, and a **three-year term or until age 70**.
notes.61: Know the NHRC's powers and limits. It can inquire, visit jails, intervene in court with approval and recommend compensation, but its recommendations are not binding. The rule most missed: **no inquiry into matters more than one year old** under section 36(2). Help people file early and keep a dated record.
notes.62: Use the four steps: document, file within one year, follow up, escalate. State commissions handle matters in the state lists, and section 30 allows a Human Rights Court in each district. Since 2006 the NHRC can transfer a complaint to the state commission, so **filing with the state commission first often saves time**.
notes.63: The Paris Principles ask for a broad mandate, independence and pluralism. GANHRI grades A for fully compliant and B for partially. India's NHRC was accredited A, but its re-accreditation was deferred and a downgrade to B recommended in March 2025, with review postponed to November 2026. **Check the latest decision before you cite its status.**
notes.64: Compare the neighbours' institutions and GANHRI status. Nepal and Pakistan hold A, Sri Lanka returned to A from its first session in 2024, and Bangladesh holds B with members resigned in November 2024. Statuses can change at any session, so **note the date of the source** when you quote one.
notes.65: Learn one route to court per neighbour: Bangladesh Article 102, Pakistan Articles 199 and 184(3), Sri Lanka Article 126 and Nepal Article 46 with 133 and 144. Sri Lanka's one-month limit is short, and the time runs from the infringement. In every country **check limitation periods before advising anyone**.
notes.67: The right to food moved from a court case, PUCL (WP 196 of 2001), to a statute, the NFSA 2013. Learn the five entitlements and their sections: 3(2) coverage, 3(1) 5 kg, the Antyodaya proviso, section 4 for pregnant and lactating women, and 5(1)(b) mid-day meals. A statutory entitlement can be **claimed and enforced** through a grievance route.
notes.68: Stunting measures long-term undernutrition. India's 29.3 per cent comes from NFHS-6, down from 35.5, and the other countries come from different survey years, so the comparison is indicative. A rights reading asks whether the **minimum core** is met, whether the trend is down, and whether the poorest improve as fast as the average.
notes.69: Paschim Banga (1996) turned on a man refused at several hospitals. The Court held it breached Article 21 and that lack of resources cannot excuse failing to provide emergency treatment. Compare Nepal, where the 2015 Constitution makes basic health care a right in Article 35, and Bangladesh, where Article 8 leaves that Part **unenforceable in court**.
notes.70: Two legal changes reshape work on the right to work. The rural employment guarantee Act was repealed from 1 July 2026 and replaced by the Viksit Bharat G RAM G Act 2025 with 125 days of work, and the four Labour Codes came into force on 21 November 2025. Read the new texts **before advising anyone**.
notes.71: India's Constitution names no right to housing, but Olga Tellis tied livelihood and shelter to Article 21 and required fair procedure. Use the checklist before any eviction: notice, hearing or survey, resettlement near work and schools, safe timing, records. The deck labels it illustrative, so **call a lawyer as soon as a notice appears**.
notes.72: Borrow the OHCHR structure of structural, process and outcome indicators. For education, Article 21A and the RTE Act are structural, the share of RTE 25 per cent seats filled is process, and Class 8 completion by girls, Dalit and Adivasi children is outcome. **Disaggregation turns an ordinary indicator into a rights indicator**.
notes.73: ICESCR Article 2(1) makes budgets evidence. Ask four questions of any budget: is the allocation enough for the entitlement, was money released on time and spent, do needier districts receive more, did allocation fall in real terms. A cut needs justification under progressive realisation. Use **published documents and RTI**.
notes.75: Read the table across: for speech, assembly and association it lists the ICCPR article, the Indian clause and the permitted grounds for restriction. The deck states the law as of October 2026 and judges no case. You need it because it governs **how an NGO is funded, how staff can speak and what risks communities take**.
notes.76: Follow the four steps from section 124A to the BNS. The Supreme Court order of 11 May 2022 asked governments to refrain from FIRs under 124A while it was reconsidered. The BNS has no offence named sedition, and section 152 punishes acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity. Courts are still reading it, so **check current case law**.
notes.77: Three UAPA features matter after an arrest: individuals can be designated terrorists under section 35, section 43D(5) restricts bail, and section 43D(2) allows investigation to extend to 180 days. In Najeeb (2021) the Court held the bail bar softens where trial cannot end in reasonable time. **Constitutional courts can still grant bail** for Part III violations.
notes.78: The 2020 amendment changed four FCRA rules: no transfer of foreign contribution to others, administrative expenses capped at 20 per cent, Aadhaar or passport of office bearers, and receipt only in the specified SBI New Delhi account. The Court upheld these in Noel Harper (2022). The effect on partnerships: **no sub-granting of foreign funds**.
notes.79: RTI section 7(1) requires a reply in 30 days, or 48 hours for life or liberty. The DPDP Act substituted section 8(1)(j) from 13 November 2025, removing the public-interest override, and the Supreme Court issued notice on 26 May 2026. Frame requests around **aggregate and scheme-level records**: budgets, sanction orders, stock registers, inspection reports.
notes.80: Use the quarterly checklist as protection for the people you work with. It covers FCRA, data, speech, staff safety and partners. A lapsed registration or an accounting error can end a programme and expose communities. The deck labels the table illustrative, so **use a chartered accountant and a lawyer** for specifics.
notes.81: Plan for retaliation before you ask anyone to speak, and keep the decision with the person at risk. Before: map who might retaliate, explain risks, agree what is recorded. During: collect only what you need. After: record at once, contact a lawyer, consider an SHRC complaint inside the one-year limit. **Use UN routes with consent**.
notes.83: Learn the three pillars: the state duty to protect, the corporate responsibility to respect, and access to remedy. The Council endorsed the UNGPs on 16 June 2011. They are not a treaty, and their force comes from national law, company policies, investor rules and supply-chain contracts. **Principle 11** carries the responsibility to respect.
notes.84: Principle 17 asks enterprises to carry out human rights due diligence. The four steps are assess, integrate, track and communicate. For an NGO partnering with a company, **ask to see the due diligence** on the site you will work in. For a community it supplies the question: has the company assessed its impact on us?
notes.85: Use Principle 31's eight criteria as tests of any complaints system: legitimate, accessible, predictable, equitable, transparent, rights-compatible, a source of learning and based on dialogue. Each has a field test, such as whether workers would use it without fear. They apply equally to **your own NGO's system** and to government portals.
notes.86: Status check for October 2026: the National Action Plan on Business and Human Rights was a zero draft in 2019 and is not adopted; the 2018 guidelines underlie SEBI's BRSR, mandatory for the top 1,000 from FY 2022-23; Section 135 CSR is in force; the Labour Codes took effect 21 November 2025. **BRSR disclosures are public**, so read them before partnering.
notes.87: On 24 April 2013 Rana Plaza collapsed near Dhaka, killing more than 1,100 garment workers. The question of whether a brand answers for its suppliers moved into buyer contracts, investor questions and law-making. The lesson for programmes: audits failed, so strengthen **worker voice**, the ability to refuse unsafe work and report without retaliation.
notes.88: Sort NGO roles into those that work and those to avoid. Good roles: document impacts, translate commitments, monitor independently if communities ask, and review due diligence before a CSR partnership. Avoid running a company's grievance system, using CSR to replace state duties with no exit plan, signing gag terms, or speaking without a mandate. **Put the agreement and exit plan in writing.**
notes.90: Run this check at design stage and again at mid-term. Each question links to a part of the deck, and a no is a design task whose answers belong in the proposal. Start with who the duty-bearers are, by name and office, and end with **who sustains the gains after the project**.
notes.91: The Bihar case is hypothetical. Read each row left to right: problem, right and source, duty-bearer, action. Ration loss maps to the NFSA, dropout to Article 21A, unpaid wages to the Labour Codes and bondage to Article 23. The shape to copy: **every row has a law, a named office and an action**.
notes.92: Choose the route to match the problem. Each row gives a first route, a fallback and one thing to avoid, such as going to court first when a written application would work. Remember the one-year limit for police abuse complaints and that a PIL needs the affected people's consent. The table is **illustrative guidance, not legal advice**.
notes.93: Documentation has three parts: what to record, how, and what to avoid. Record who, what, when, where, officials' names and documents, with consent in the person's language. Avoid leading questions, promises and sharing names on messaging groups. DPDP duties apply from 13 May 2027, and **laws on child victims restrict disclosing identities**.
notes.94: Write the letter in five parts: facts, entitlement, duty, request, record. The illustrative letter cites section 3(1) of the NFSA, names 14 households, and asks for restoration within 15 days. A letter that names the law and asks for a **dated action** is harder to ignore than one that asks for help.
notes.95: Turn delivery indicators into rights indicators by changing what they measure. Children enrolled becomes completion of Class 8 by sex, caste and disability. Trainings held becomes grievances resolved within the legal time limit. The rights column measures **duty-bearer performance and equality of access**. Disaggregate every people-level indicator by at least sex, caste or tribe, and disability.
notes.96: Plan for retaliation, lost benefits, exposed identities, legal risk to staff and raised expectations. Mitigate with consent at each step, collective complaints where safer, data minimisation, sourced statements and honest explanation. Remember the closing rule: the person whose rights were violated decides whether to complain, and the programme **makes options and risks clear**.
notes.98: Use the eight points as a closing checklist. On the law: a right is a claim with a duty-bearer and remedy, India is party to six of nine treaties, Article 21 with Part IV carries most social rights, and treaties enter courts where law is silent. On practice: start at home, file within one year, measure performance, **plan for retaliation**.
notes.99: Pick your next course by need. Indian Constitution 101 covers Parts III and IV, Child Rights 101 the CRC, Governance & Accountability 101 RTI and grievance systems, and Digital Rights & AI 101 privacy. The suggested order is Indian Constitution, Governance & Accountability, then Advocacy Basics, with **Child Rights before any work with children**.
